Long coupon bond2 / 2 / 10296.68

Between zero and the first node, interpolate log discounts linearly. This makes r = −log D(0.5)/0.5 constant over the entire option life. The later nodes fund later reserve cash. Do not use the 1.5-year spot rate as the put's six-month funding rate, or infer a future physical short-rate forecast from the forward curve. The fixed-income method source supports matching cash characteristics and dates; the selected interpolation and all case quotes are ours.

The alternative reserve is a different issuer's bond with scheduled cash 3, 3, 103. Its stipulated pricing law has survival probability 0.9 and default probability 0.1. Default occurs at year 1 before that coupon; only the year-0.5 coupon has been received. No further coupon or face is paid. Recovery is 40% of face, paid at year 1.5. Default does not reduce Alder's obligations. These are two states with an exogenous pricing probability, not an estimated physical hazard or a legal statement about an actual bond.

Required work and submission

  1. Contract and information register. Submit the cash schedule, exercise filtration, units, issued-versus-held position signs, interpolation, trading permissions and all excluded costs. Identify which inputs are quotes, which are model choices and which are unweighted scenarios. Draw the dependency flow. Explain why linear addition of the fixed and put values does not require independence of their cash amounts.
  2. Curve, valuation and rate hedge. Bootstrap and reprice all three instruments exactly. Value the fixed promise; compute interval simple forward rates, continuous node rates, key-rate dollar exposures, parallel duration and the parallel second derivative. Buy the cash-matched zeros. Separately construct a two-zero barbell at 0.5 and 1.5 matching initial PV and parallel first derivative. Reprice liability and barbell under the four supplied zero-rate shifts. Derive a second-order residual with an explicit remainder bound and explain why that barbell is neither a universal curve hedge nor automatically a dated cash reserve.
  3. Continuous reference and finite exercise. Derive the discounted-stock martingale and pricing equation under the stated constant-parameter model, with the growth/integrability qualifications taught in Chapters 7–8. Price the put and call, check parity, and compute put delta, gamma and vega. Independently integrate the normal payoff. Implement the 4/8/16/32-step trees, reproduce the coarsest root stock/cash hedge and every early-exercise decision, and compare European/Bermudan/American prices on each fixed grid. Explain exactly what cross-grid comparisons do not prove.
  4. Simulation evidence. Implement exact terminal GBM simulation, plain, antithetic and fixed-control estimates using the documented seed experiment. Derive their expectations, variance expressions and correct sample units. Reconcile analytic price, quadrature difference, tree difference and sample SE. Report both approximate CLT intervals and the scoped bounded-put Hoeffding calculation. Do not replace an independent benchmark with saved output, call paired payoffs independent, or describe the finite pseudo generator as exact iid continuous randomness.
  5. Funded discrete hedge. Rebalance the analytic put delta on the supplied times for every supplied stock history. Start with the analytic premium, finance every stock trade, compound the bank balance, liquidate at T, and pay the put. Charge 0.001 times absolute stock notional on entry, each rebalance and liquidation. Reconcile zero-cost and with-cost errors by the dated cost identity. Explain why the five path results neither estimate expected profit nor establish a continuous volatility-mismatch formula. Calculate the additional initial cash needed to keep the worst tested terminal error above −1 CU.
  6. Credit reserve and funding. Price survival and default cash at their actual dates. Reconcile the apparent reserve saving with the expected pricing-law loss. Build the default funding account, showing the missed coupon, terminal shortfall and bridge interest. State the first date on which an unavailable credit line would cause failure. Do not spend a risk-adjusted expected value as if it were a sure payment.
  7. Decision and controls. Reproduce all five stated classroom gates below, report every failure, and give a one-page recommendation. Separate the frictionless model quote, transaction costs, tested-path capital, contractual changes and unmodeled funding/credit risks. Propose a restricted demonstration, redesign or refusal with a named evidence requirement and trigger for reconsideration. A defensible refusal can earn full credit; no client is assumed willing to pay a larger quote.
  8. Independent reproduction and transfer. Deliver readable standard-library code, complete inputs/output, a cash/evidence ledger, a source-scope note and a tests log. Verify quiet import/API and normal/optimized portable execution. Solve all six transfer tasks below and defend one selected by the examiner without looking up the reference answer. Preserve the baseline; record what changed, what stayed fixed and why. Explain one material limitation of each independent check.

The report should link each recommendation to a specific cash identity, numerical comparison or stated assumption. Include the full dated ledgers as attachments rather than replacing them with prose. A useful error register has separate rows for exact arithmetic/implementation, deterministic approximation, ideal sampling uncertainty, finite pseudo-generator error, model identification and contractual ambiguity. A smaller number in one row does not resolve a problem in another. The methods follow finite stopping, Itô calculus, continuous valuation, funded Greeks, numerical evidence and controlled use.

The stipulated demonstration gates

Require all five: (1) requested put rights remain European; (2) the proposed reserve funds every declared payment date without an injection, with cash-matched riskless zeros satisfying this by construction; (3) the quote covers max(fixed-riskless PV, actual selected reserve purchase PV) plus analytic put plus the additional initial cash calculated from the −1 CU tested-loss limit; (4) controlled estimated MC SE is at most 0.15 CU; and (5) the finest European tree differs from the analytic European put by at most 0.03 CU. The maximum preserves the conservative riskless-liability floor and also finances a selected reserve that costs more. Equality passes; the floating quote comparison allows 10−10 CU numerical tolerance. These are author-designed classroom rules. They are neither an optimized commercial risk policy nor regulatory approval. A failure cannot be averaged away by four other passes.

Passing means eligible for a limited classroom demonstration. It does not validate the return process, prove a loss bound outside supplied paths, establish a borrowable credit line, clear a changed exercise contract or authorize a real trade. The root continuation hedge is not an instruction to continue after an optimal immediate exercise. The same distinction between a computation and its permitted use must appear in your own interface.

Fresh transfer tasks

  1. Quote propagation. Increase only the long calibration instrument's quote from 96.68 to 96.70. Before running code, derive the exact change in the last discount, fixed-liability PV and risky-reserve PV. Does the put reference change? Distinguish rebuilding a barbell from repricing an already held barbell.
  2. Same terminal payoff, different trading. Replace the round-trip path 100, 85, 95, 110, 90 by 100, 100, 100, 100, 90. Compare funded hedge errors with the same terminal put payment. Then allow trading only at time zero and maturity for both histories. Explain the resulting equality and why it does not show that less frequent hedging is universally better.
  3. Recovery date and a real bridge cost. Move the 40 recovery from year 1.5 to year 1, after default but available before that date's liability payment. Recompute reserve PV and the full default funding account. Restore delayed recovery and add a 200-basis-point annual continuous borrowing spread to the negative bank balance over years 1–1.5; calculate the additional terminal cost. This spread is a separately specified extension, not part of the baseline code.
  4. Recovery and apparent savings. Restore the baseline dates and raise recovery to 100% of face. Does that fund all promised coupons? Separately restore recovery 40 and retain the entire 6.018 CU reserve discount in the bank at time zero. Is that enough to fund the default state? Give the remaining terminal deficit, not just an expectation.
  5. Wrong-sign control and changed rights. Change the fixed control coefficient to +1. Determine from the covariance formula whether variance improves under the ideal baseline law; then inspect the seeded result without selecting a favorable seed. Request American rights while keeping the European reference module and quote 119. Does a larger quote alone pass the contract gate?
  6. A limited repair and its boundary. Use cash-matched zeros and quote 119, retaining the baseline European rights and numerical budgets. Show which gates now pass and what they establish. Double proportional trading costs and derive the terminal-error change without simulating new normals. Name an additional path or funding assumption that must be tested before broadening the allowed use.

Five essential domains; partial credit follows the displayed allocation

Advancement requires at least 85/100 overall and 15/20 in every domain, satisfactory transfer/teach-back, and remediation of every critical error. These are the library author's criteria. Award fractional credit, carry a transparent arithmetic slip through later work without repeated deductions, and score a new reasoning error separately. Alternative policy choices earn full credit when they first reproduce the assigned calculation and then state the changed premise, consequence and evidence requirement.

Critical errors override the total: funding a payment with money received later without showing borrowing; treating reserve default as cancellation of the client obligation; using the wrong curve tenor; exercising with future stock information; pricing an American contract with terminal-only European sampling; treating antithetic legs as independent sample units; using a selected confidence interval as a model or legal guarantee; resetting hedge wealth by an undisclosed injection; omitting stock entry or liquidation costs; treating the expected credit discount as a sure reserve; or declaring all-path safety from five scenarios. Require corrected code/ledger, an explanation of the mechanism and a fresh transfer, not merely a revised headline number.

Complete instructor guide, numerical benchmarks and transfer answers

1. Contract map and exact curve

The fixed and put cash add because present valuation is linear. Their statistical independence is unnecessary. Default of the reserve issuer changes an asset cash stream, while the liability schedule remains 3, 3, 103 plus the separately owed put. The bank/stock positions hedge the put liability; positive put delta is not the correct sign here. The price received at time zero must be allocated among the dated reserve, option hedge and any added cash budget before profit is discussed.

Triangular calibration gives D1 = 98/100 = 49/50, D2 = (100.79 − 3D1)/103 = 19/20, and D3 = (96.68 − 2D1 − 2D2)/102 = 91/100. Substitution returns every quote exactly. Fixed PV is 3(.98) + 3(.95) + 103(.91) = 99.52, with pieces 2.94, 2.85 and 93.73. Holding zeros paying 3, 3, 103 matches each dated liability without future sales. This is stronger than matching one yield or one duration.

The simple interval forward rates are 2/49, 6/95 and 8/91 per year. For example, .98/.95 is the bank gross growth over years 0.5–1, so its simple annualized rate is (.98/.95 − 1)/.5 = 6/95. Continuous node rates are approximately .040405415, .051293294 and .062873786. These describe the selected deterministic curve. They do not separate expected physical rate movements from a term premium or identify a stochastic-rate process.

2. Rate derivatives, barbell and a controlled remainder

For a node-zero-rate perturbation zj, PV is Σ cjDje−tjzj. Its negative first node derivatives are 1.47, 2.85 and 140.595 CU-years. Parallel dollar duration is 144.915 CU-years, normalized duration 28983/19904 ≈ 1.45614 years, and the parallel second derivative is 214.4775 CU-years². These are continuous-zero-rate sensitivities, not modified duration with an unstated periodic-yield convention.

Let A and B be the barbell's present-value allocations to dates .5 and 1.5. Solve A + B = 99.52 and .5A + 1.5B = 144.915, giving A = 4.365 and B = 95.155. The zero face quantities are 873/196 ≈ 4.454082 and 19031/182 ≈ 104.565934. Its middle-date quantity is zero. The asset-minus-liability key exposures are g = (57/80, −57/20, 171/80) = (.7125, −2.85, 2.1375), summing to zero. A parallel first-order change therefore cancels; a general vector change need not.

Let aj = barbell cashj − liability cashj. Surplus = Σ ajDj[−tjzj + ½(tjzj)²] + R, because Σ ajDj = 0.
|R| ≤ Σ |aj|Dje|tjzj||tjzj|³/6.

This follows from the ordinary exponential Taylor theorem applied separately to each finite cash term; it requires no stochastic-rate convergence theorem. For parallel h, the second surplus derivative is Σ tjgj = .7125. At h = ±.01 the second-order surplus is .000035625. Exact upward/downward surpluses are .000035270599 and .000035983112. Under the twist (−.01, 0, .01), first-order surplus is −.01425 and exact surplus is −.014072643841. Raising only the middle zero rate .01 gives exact surplus .028357973815. The positive parallel curvature does not protect against that twist.

The barbell is not the cash reserve. At year 1 it has no maturity receipt, while the client is owed 3. An actual implementation would have to preserve earlier surplus, sell/rebalance later assets or establish borrowing under explicit future-price and permission assumptions. The project instead funds the fixed sleeve with matched zeros. No mark-to-market surplus has been counted as immediately available cash.

3. Constant-rate reference and finite stopping

Over the put's life, r = −2 log(.98). Under the stated Q law, St = 100 exp[(r − σ²/2)t + σWt]. Applying the proved scalar Itô formula to the exponential gives dS = rSdt + σSdW. The normalized exponential has mean one by the Gaussian moment-generating function, so E[e−rtSt] = 100. Its finite second moment makes the discounted stock integral a true martingale on the finite horizon. This step requires the Gaussian model and bounded constant coefficient, not just notation calling a process a local martingale.

For a C1,2 interior option value, hold VS shares and bank cash V − SVS; self-financing gains and Itô give Vt + rSVS + ½σ²S²VSS − rV = 0. The put has terminal payoff (K − S)+, boundary V(t,0) = Ke−r(T−t) and vanishing value as S grows. The continuous at-most-linear-growth solution and stopped/martingale justification are those proved in Chapter 8; this project does not infer uniqueness from a numerical grid. The primary Black–Scholes notes supply context, not empirical validation.

Here d1 = −.0733267291 and d2 = −.2501034244. The put K D(T)Φ(−d2) − S0Φ(−d1) is 8.688302035018 CU; the call is 5.788302035018. Call minus put is 100 − 105(.98) = −2.9. Put delta is −.529226938909, gamma .022506994028 per CU, and vega 28.133742534727 CU per unit volatility, or about .281337425 per one-percentage-point volatility change. The frictionless model quote for the whole obligation is 108.208302035018; fees and loss capital are separate.

At each node, p = (R − d)/(u − d) with d < R < u. Discount the conditional successor value by R; on allowed exercise dates take its maximum with the immediate payoff. Backward induction proves the finite Snell value: any adapted stopping policy is bounded by this recursion, and first optimal exercise attains it. Ties may continue. On a fixed tree, including more dates enlarges the permissible policies. Changing n also changes the stock law, so the displayed descending prices do not prove that CRR convergence is universally monotone or establish a general rate for kinked payoffs.

The four-step European root hedge holds −.530119757175 shares and 61.929464580684 bank cash, costing 8.917488863234. At the first down/up states it produces 13.715597332537 and 4.332108496747, respectively. Financing the stock trade is essential to these equalities. In the four-step all-node contract, early exercise occurs at step 2 with zero up-moves (S ≈ 83.796689), and at step 3 with zero or one up-move (S ≈ 76.707934 or 91.540531). The middle early node is the sole positive early-exercise choice for the Bermudan version. Coarsest full-history enumeration has 677 all-node stopping-policy constructions, obtained from a0 = 1 and am+1 = 1 + am², and 17 Bermudan constructions; their best expected discounted payments independently reproduce the recursion. This is finite verification alongside the proof, not an infinite-horizon theorem. The discrete-market source is used within that scope.

4. Numerical and sampling evidence

The lognormal terminal payoff integral is an independent anchor. Put its kink at z* = [log(K/S0) − (r − σ²/2)T]/(σ√T), integrate the smooth positive-payoff part, and retain the discarded normal tails in the error register. The toolkit's 256/512-interval Simpson values are 8.688302327905 and 8.688302053310. Their difference is −2.74594 × 10−7; the fine value differs from the analytic formula by 1.82927 × 10−8. Because the put is bounded by KD = 102.9 after discounting, both omitted tails are at most 2KDΦ(−10) ≈ 1.56817 × 10−21. That is a genuine ideal-law tail bound. The Simpson refinement difference is a diagnostic, not a rigorously certified integration error. Independent adaptive integration gives approximately 8.688302035019.

Y = e−rT(K − ST)+, X = e−rTST, E[X] = S0.
Yβ = Y − β(X − S0), E[Yβ] = E[Y], Var(Yβ) = Var(Y) + β²Var(X) − 2βCov(Y,X).
A(Z) = [Y(Z) + Y(−Z)]/2, E[A] = E[Y], Var(A) = [Var(Y) + Cov(Y(Z),Y(−Z))]/2.

Square-integrability follows from finite lognormal moments. The fixed β = −.5 gives Y + .5(X − 100), not Y − .5(X − 100). An increasing control and decreasing put have negative covariance; for the particular ideal baseline, independent payoff integration yields Var(Y) ≈ 106.463456912, Cov(Y,X) ≈ −156.753973262, controlled variance ≈ 29.068002398, and antithetic-pair variance ≈ 16.797720226. This supports the chosen coefficient in this case, not a universal improvement for arbitrary β. If β were estimated, an independent pilot or a separately justified estimation scheme would be required. The reference uses no fitted coefficient.

Seed 271828; each estimator individually uses 4,096 payoff evaluations

Plain4,096 single payoffs8.560204768.163819942[8.239117681, 8.881291854]

Plain and controlled observations use both ideal independent Box–Muller normals per base draw. Antithetics use the cosine normal and its negative as one pair; counting 4,096 independent antithetic units would understate SE. The three estimators share inputs and are not independent experiments. At equal payoff count, the ideal pair-to-plain mean-variance ratio is 2Var(A)/Var(Y), not Var(A)/Var(Y). Sample comparisons should also include computing cost before claiming general efficiency.

At fixed n ideal independent units, s²/(n) estimates mean variance and the CLT motivates mean ± 1.96s/√n asymptotically. For plain and pair payoffs in [0,KD], the previously proved Hoeffding inequality gives ideal coverage at least .95 with half-width KD√[log(40)/(2n)]: 2.183572593 for the plain sample and 3.088037976 for pairs using this deliberately loose common bound. The controlled payoff is unbounded, so that same bound cannot be copied to it. The SHA256/open-midpoint generator produces a reproducible finite pseudo experiment, not a proof of iid continuous-normal coverage. A seeded interval may miss the truth; changing seeds until it contains the analytic price invalidates the stated experiment. These distinctions follow the scoped output-analysis and variance-reduction sources.

5. Every trade is funded

Let δi be the analytic put delta chosen at ti for the interval until the next date; set δ−1 = 0 and δN = 0 for entry and liquidation. Start with P0 = 8.688302035018. The bank immediately after entry is P0 − δ0S0 − κ|δ0|S0. Accrue that balance before each later trade, then deduct (δi − δi−1)Si + κ|δi − δi−1|Si. At T liquidate first, then pay (105 − ST)+. No rebalance deposits enough outside cash to reset the account to a fresh option mark.

D(T)ET = P0 + Σi=1…N δi−1[D(ti)Si − D(ti−1)Si−1] − D(T)(K − ST)+ − Σi=0…N D(ti)κ|δi − δi−1|Si.

Discount each self-financing bank equation and telescope to obtain this identity. It is an independent cash audit, not a small-change approximation. Since this delta rule does not depend on the bank balance, the zero-cost error minus with-cost error equals the terminal value of all costs. There is no extra profit from the short-stock proceeds: they already enter the bank alongside the liability to buy back stock.

6. A cheap reserve is not the same promise

The survival cash is (3,3,103); default cash is (3,0,40). Default PV is 3(.98) + 40(.91) = 39.34. The risky asset price is .9(99.52) + .1(39.34) = 93.502. Its 6.018 CU discount equals .1 times the 60.18 CU default-state PV loss. No physical default estimate or independence assumption between equity and default is needed for this two-state marginal calculation. A joint risk model would be needed for a joint portfolio loss distribution.

7. Decision, evidence and limitations

The baseline passes the European-rights gate, controlled SE gate (.085861373 ≤ .15) and finest European tree comparison (|8.706023840303 − 8.688302035018| ≈ .017721805 ≤ .03). It fails dated reserve funding and the quote's tested-loss budget: 108.5 < 118.944870090400. The correct output is revise_before_demo, with both failures visible. The 6.018 reserve discount must not be subtracted from the cash reserve needed to honor the client obligation.

The reserve purchase cost must also be covered when it exceeds the riskless floor. Set all three coupons to zero and specify default and full-face recovery at the first date, .5. The riskless promise costs 100(.91) = 91, but the selected risky reserve costs .9(91) + .1[100(.98)] = 91.7. Its signed apparent_initial_saving is −.7. The early 100 funds every later fixed payment in default, leaving 100/13 at year 1.5, but that future, default-only excess cannot pay for the initial reserve purchase or fund the hedge in survival. The required quote is therefore 91.7 + 8.688302035018 + 10.736568055382 = 111.124870090400. Quote 110.5 fails funding alone; at the allowed eight decimal places, 111.12487009 still fails and 111.12487010 passes the five classroom gates. Selecting matched zeros instead costs 91 and lowers the threshold to 110.424870090400, so 110.5 passes for that selection. The output records both selected_reserve_pv and reserve_budget_pv; the separately labeled frictionless model quote continues to use the riskless fixed-liability reference.

A defensible memo declines the current package. It offers a limited demonstration only with matched zeros, adequate separately allocated initial hedge cash, unchanged European rights and the stated computational evidence. It requests execution/funding terms and a broader, justified path model before any larger use. An alternative is to simplify the promise or refuse the proposed commercial quote. Higher client willingness to pay, a guaranteed hedge and a real financing facility are not created by a passing JSON flag.

For independent validation, solve the calibration as a simultaneous linear system; price European trees by terminal binomial sums; enumerate the four-step stopping policies; integrate the Gaussian payoff with a method different from the implementation; reconstruct discounted hedge gains rather than repeating the bank loop; and compute reserve funding from cumulative discounted cash deficits. These checks isolate implementation mistakes. They do not identify the correct future law or contract, establish empirical coverage or replace human judgment. The reference checker also exercises negative rates, altered quotes, recovery times, stock histories, costs, control signs and exercise requests, and rejects malformed or out-of-domain inputs under normal and optimized execution.

8. Complete transfer answers and scoring guidance

  1. Quote propagation. The first two discounts remain fixed. ΔD3 = .02/102 = 1/5100. The fixed PV rises by 103/5100 ≈ .020196078431. The risky asset has expected final cash .9(103) + .1(40) = 96.7, so its PV rises by 967/51000 ≈ .018960784314. The first-segment rate and European put do not change. Rebuilding the duration-matched barbell solves new equations and changes positions; repricing an existing hedge holds positions fixed. Conflating those operations hides hedge turnover.

  2. Trading history. Both round-trip and calm-history paths end at 90 and owe 15 on the put. The calm-history zero-cost/with-cost errors are 1.806685410882 and 1.677445349078, versus −11.780478695425 and −11.955681689165 on the original path. Interior stock trades explain the difference. With only entry and liquidation, both yield .237938687906 before costs and .136305514536 after costs because the same starting holding is carried between the same endpoints. This is a conditional two-history comparison; other paths can favor frequent adjustment, and costs and permissions must stay fixed when testing frequency.

  3. Recovery timing and bridge spread. Immediate recovery produces default cash (3,40,0), PV 40.94 and risky PV 93.662, a .16 CU increase. At year 1 the bank is 40 − 3 = 37; at year 1.5 it is 37(.95/.91) − 103 = −5858/91 ≈ −64.373626374. It no longer needs the year-1 bridge, but still fails the last payment. Restore delayed recovery: adding a continuous .02 spread to the borrowed 3 for half a year adds 3(.95/.91)(e.02×.5 − 1) ≈ .031475798011 CU to the terminal deficit, beyond the baseline .131868132 bridge interest. This is a funding-cost extension, not a change in the recovery cash or the baseline risk-neutral asset PV.

  4. Face is not every coupon. Full face recovery at year 1.5 gives default cash (3,0,100), still losing 3 at year 1 and 3 at year 1.5. Default PV loss is 5.58 and terminal deficit 558/91 ≈ 6.131868132. Restoring recovery 40 and putting the 6.018 initial saving into the bank changes the terminal balance to (6.018 − 60.18)/.91 = −27081/455 ≈ −59.518681319. It can cover the earlier 3 CU gap but not the whole default state. An expected discount is too small to collateralize its much larger conditional loss.

  5. Wrong sign and wrong rights. At β = +1 the ideal variance is Var(Y) + Var(X) − 2Cov(Y,X) ≈ 737.405478428, versus plain 106.463456912. A fixed control remains unbiased under the ideal law even when it makes variance worse. The seeded output must be reported without searching for a favorable exception. A request for American rights fails exercise_matches_european_reference even at quote 119: the numerical tree comparison is available, but neither the terminal-only MC nor the European Greek hedge has become an American valuation/hedging proof.

  6. Limited repair. Matched zeros and quote 119 satisfy all five baseline gates. The quote exceeds the tested threshold by about .055129909600 CU at time zero; no all-path guarantee follows. Doubling κ while retaining the same delta rule doubles each path's PV/terminalized cost, so its with-cost error falls by one additional copy of the original terminalized cost. For the round trip, that decrement is .175202993740 CU and the new error is approximately −12.130884682906. Independent funding or a new path is still required to justify broader use; examples include an unavailable short-stock borrow, a new large reversal between hedge dates, an execution spread changing with volatility, or an early exercise request. A proposed extension earns full credit only when it identifies the changed cash/model assumption and a check that could reveal failure.

Instructor judgment. Require the supplied contract to be solved before accepting an alternative. Award policy points for a reasoned refusal as readily as for a narrow demonstration; demand the same numerical transparency from both. For the oral defense, change one input without revealing its expected direction and ask the learner to trace the consequences through the funding ledger and decision. A correct prediction with a stated limitation is stronger evidence than memorizing the reference output. The complete source, code and review packet supports reproducibility. Separate peer/coordinator review is an acceptance gate; it does not certify an individual learner's mastery.

Oral transfer and teach-back

Use the following five transfers after the written work and project. Allow about ten minutes per domain, with paper and a basic calculator. The examiner may change one stated input after the initial answer; the learner must identify what changes and what remains invariant. Each transfer is worth four points: one for the quantitative or formal core, one for a complete cash or information argument, one for its assumptions/limits, and one for a coherent response to the changed input. Pass at 17/20 with at least three points in every transfer and no unresolved critical error. This protocol supports human assessment; the library does not claim that a learner has already performed it.

  1. Rate matching is local. A liability and a hedge both have value 100 CU and first derivative −200 CU per unit parallel yield shift. Their second derivatives are respectively 500 and 300. Starting from zero surplus, estimate hedge-minus-liability surplus after a 0.01 parallel increase through second order. Does initial value/duration matching immunize every shock? Transfer: explain what must be added before drawing a conclusion about a nonparallel curve move.
  2. Cash arrives on dates. A desk has five CU immediately available. It must post three as initial margin and then pay a four-CU variation loss before receiving a six-CU separate settlement tomorrow. Borrowing and collateral release are unavailable today. Reconcile today's gap and explain why tomorrow's receipt does not remove it. Transfer: a confirmed two-CU facility becomes drawable before variation is due, but has an interest charge; state which conclusion changes and which valuation/cost questions remain.
  3. A nonlinear function needs the Itô term. Under a specified pricing law, dS=0.02Sdt+0.30SdW with no dividend. Derive d(S²) and the drift of e−0.02tS². For a claim paying S₁² and S₀=10, calculate its discounted expectation using the GBM second moment. Transfer: explain why zero discounted stock drift does not make every nonlinear discounted stock function a martingale.
  4. Inversion is not a joint price test. Matched zero-rate European calls with S=100 and strikes 90, 100, 110 cost 14, 9 and 5. Test the normalized butterfly. Change only the middle quote to 10 and repeat. Both middle quotes lie inside their individual inversion bounds. Explain why that fact does not decide the butterfly question, and why a passing finite screen still does not identify a dynamic volatility law.
  5. Fit does not identify the requested use. A price family is P(t)=100−t+c·t(t−1), per 100 CU future payment. Calibration at years 0 and 1 is exact for every c. Under an explicitly imposed −0.25≤c≤0.25, find the year-2 range. A policy permits a range no wider than 0.25 CU for point valuation. Give a decision, a responsible remediation and a closure test. Transfer: explain what changes if use is restricted to year 1.
Oral answer standards
  1. The value and first-order terms cancel. The second-order surplus is ½(300−500)(0.01)²=−0.01 CU. Equal value and duration therefore do not imply protection from every parallel shock; curvature and higher terms matter. Nonparallel shifts require the actual curve coordinates, key-rate sensitivities or a stated model of curve moves, and possibly cross-curvature. The examiner can reverse the shock: this quadratic term keeps its sign. A correct response distinguishes a local approximation from a global guarantee and identifies the missing exposure rather than asserting that more duration precision would solve it.
  2. After posting initial margin only two CU remain; paying four creates a two-CU funding gap. The six-CU future settlement may improve later wealth but cannot settle today's obligation under the stated rights. A usable earlier two-CU facility closes this immediate gap, subject to its actual draw and repayment terms. Its interest, any commitment fees, collateral rights and future repayment then belong in the funded ledger; access to financing does not erase economic cost or counterparty risk. The answer must keep initial collateral, variation settlement and unrelated receipts distinct.
  3. Itô gives d(S²)=(2·0.02+0.30²)S²dt+2(0.30)S²dW=0.13S²dt+0.60S²dW. Discounting leaves drift 0.11e−0.02tS²dt. The discounted expectation is 100e0.11≈111.627807046. This uses the stipulated Q and finite GBM moments; it is not the physical forecast under an unspecified law. Discounted stock is a martingale because its linear function has zero second derivative. Curvature creates the additional term for S². A general growth/uniqueness theorem has not been proved merely by naming that expectation.
  4. The normalized butterfly costs ½(14+5)−9=0.5 CU, which passes this nonnegative-cost test. At middle quote 10 it costs −0.5 CU, although all three individual inversion bounds still pass. Buying the two half-sized wing calls and selling the middle call produces a nonnegative terminal triangle and an initial receipt in the second case under executable matched rights. An individual inverse faithfully reproduces even a jointly incoherent set of prices. Finite passing quotes establish neither every missing strike/maturity condition nor a unique process; the required response names the claim each test actually addresses.
  5. P(2)=98+2c, giving [97.5,98.5] and width 1 CU. The imposed restriction supplies a scenario range, not information from the two calibration observations. The point-valuation request fails its 0.25 range criterion. Assign an owner to obtain relevant evidence or justify a narrower intended use, an independent challenger to review it, and a reproducible closure test tied to the requested target and version. Year-1 use has the common value 99 and zero range; that specific scope gate passes, while other numerical, contract and governance gates still require evidence. A committee cannot turn an unsupported parameter into an identified fact.

Delayed retention assessment

Return after 14–28 days without rereading the solutions. Allow 100 minutes with a basic calculator and the numerical inputs in these prompts. Five questions cover the five essential domains; each is worth 20 points. Pass at 85/100 with at least 15 in each and no unresolved critical error. These are new short transfers, not a substitute for either full examination. Explain a result in words after calculating it.

  1. D1 — A curve and its perturbation. A certain one-year 100-CU payment costs 97. A two-year bond paying five CU at year 1 and 105 at year 2 costs 99.35. (a, 5 points) Bootstrap the two discount factors and the effective forward rate from year 1 to 2. (b, 5) Price a certain 150-CU year-2 liability. With its continuously compounded year-2 zero rate z₂ independently shifted up by 0.002, calculate its first-order price change and exact change. (c, 5) Explain which other curve coordinates are held fixed, and why matching only sensitivity to a parallel move would not generally neutralize arbitrary key-rate shifts. (d, 5) Does this curve by itself identify the physical expectation of the future one-year short rate? Give the missing assumption or evidence.
  2. D2 — Carry and a stated credit contract. A stock costs 48. It pays a known two-CU dividend at half a year; the half-year and one-year discount factors are 0.99 and 0.94. (a, 5) Find the one-year forward delivery price and the current value of a long forward with delivery price 49, under frictionless matching rights. (b, 5) Separately, a one-year note pays 100 if it survives and 35 if it defaults, with stipulated pricing default probability 0.08 and payment always at year 1. Price the note and the discounted loss relative to a certain 100. (c, 5) A synthetic protection contract pays 65 at year 1 on that default. Its premium is 100s at year 1 only if survival occurs, with no accrual or other payments. Derive the zero-upfront annual rate s. (d, 5) Explain why the rate is neither an automatically observed physical hazard nor transferable to a contract with different accrual or settlement rules.
  3. D3 — State matching and a measure change. (a, 5) A one-period stock costs 50 and ends at 40 or 70; the bank factor is 1.05. Replicate a strike-52 call, giving shares, terminal bank cash, initial cost and pricing up probability. (b, 5) In a separate continuous model dS=0.08Sdt+0.20SdW under P with proportional yield 0.01 and bank rate 0.03, derive d log S under P and the required stock drift under Q. (c, 5) For the constant-density construction in Chapter 8, find λ so B=W+λt is Brownian under the new law; verify E exp(−λWt−λ²t/2)=1 and give the log-stock drift under Q. (d, 5) State why normalization of a density alone does not prove every discounted gain is a true martingale or establish all admissibility conditions.
  4. D4 — A mark approximation and a sampling unit. (a, 5) A desk is short 200 option units, each with supplied delta 0.45, gamma 0.02, vega 30 per unit volatility and annual calendar theta −5. Find the stock holding that offsets delta. For a spot rise of two CU, a volatility rise of 0.01 and elapsed time 1/250 year, compute the abbreviated Greek mark change per option and the combined option-plus-fixed-stock change. Treat coefficients as the stated local worksheet; do not claim an exact price or funded profit. (b, 5) Name the omitted exposure/error terms and explain what is needed to obtain financed trading profit. (c, 5) An ideal IID raw simulation has 400 observations and sample SD 6 CU. A separate antithetic run uses 200 independent pair means, each from two payoff evaluations, with sample SD 3 CU across pair means. Find both estimated standard errors and compare cost-adjusted sample variances of the means. (d, 5) Give the approximate 95% half-widths using 1.96 and explain what these intervals do not measure.
  5. D5 — A price interval and a failed use. Dates are 0 and T. A stock costs 50 and ends at (20,50,80); a certain terminal CU costs 0.95. All three states are physically possible, and unrestricted stock/cash trading is allowed only at 0 and T. A call pays (0,0,30). (a, 5) Characterize all strictly positive pricing probability vectors and derive the call's price interval. (b, 5) Give sub- and superhedges, and show why the limiting endpoints are excluded. (c, 5) A separate model comparison has candidate-minus-benchmark unit error +0.02 CU on 600 long units. The unit tolerance is 0.03 but the signed book limit is eight CU. Give the pass/fail results and effect of reducing quantity to 400. (d, 5) A size exception is still valid, but the requested version differs from the reviewed one. Write a scoped decision distinguishing the nonunique call price, the comparison error and the version gate.
Delayed retention solutions and scoring

  1. (a) D₁=0.97; 5D₁+105D₂=99.35 gives D₂=(99.35−4.85)/105=0.90. The one-year effective forward rate is D₁/D₂−1=7/90≈7.777778%. Award 1 point for D₁, 2 for the bootstrap equation/result and 2 for the correctly scaled forward.

    (b) Liability PV is 135 CU. With D₂=e−2z₂, derivative is −2(150D₂)=−270, so the first-order change is −0.54 CU. Exact change is 135(e−0.004−1)≈−0.538921439 CU. Award 1 for PV, 2 for sensitivity and 2 for exact change.

    (c) This scenario holds the one-year discount coordinate and the cash contract fixed while shifting z₂. Distinct maturity exposures need a vector of sensitivities; one scalar parallel constraint cannot generally set every component to zero. Award 2 for held-fixed coordinates, 2 for the dimension/exposure argument and 1 for a concrete nonparallel interpretation. (d) No: observed discount prices are pricing restrictions. Expectations of future short rates under P also involve risk premiums and a physical dynamics specification or evidence. An expectations hypothesis would be an additional assumption, not a fact supplied by two prices. Award 2 for the conclusion, 2 for P/Q or premium reasoning and 1 for naming the missing evidence.

  2. (a) Prepaid terminal stock costs 48−2(0.99)=46.02; forward delivery is 46.02/0.94=2301/47≈48.957446809. The existing long forward is worth 46.02−49(0.94)=−0.04 CU. Award 2 for the dividend strip, 1 for delivery and 2 for signed value.

    (b) Expected terminal receipt under the stipulated pricing law is 0.92(100)+0.08(35)=94.8; PV is 89.112. The certain 100 costs 94, leaving discounted loss 4.888 CU. Award 2 for weighted cash, 1 for PV and 2 for loss. (c) Equate 0.94·0.08·65 and 0.94·0.92·100s. Thus s=0.052/0.92=13/230≈0.056521739 per year, or about 565.217391 basis points. Award 3 for correctly dated two-leg equality and 2 for rate/units.

    (d) The law is Q as stipulated; physical default frequency and risk premiums need separate evidence. This invented contract omits default-date accrual and pays both legs at year 1. Adding accrued premium or delaying protection changes the annuity or protection PV and generally changes the fair rate. Award 2 for the physical/pricing distinction, 2 for specific changed cash rights and 1 for refusal to export the result without rebuilding them.

  3. (a) Payoffs are (0,18); Δ=18/30=0.6, terminal bank cash −24, and initial bank value −24/1.05=−160/7. Call cost is 30−160/7=50/7≈7.142857143. Pricing up probability is (1.05·50−40)/30=5/12. Award 2 for payoff matching, 1 for bank dating, 1 for cost and 1 for the probability.

    (b) Itô gives d log S=0.06dt+0.20dW. Under the pricing law the ex-dividend drift must be r−q=0.02 in the stated model. Award 3 for the quadratic-variation correction and 2 for total-gain pricing. (c) λ=(0.08+0.01−0.03)/0.20=0.3. The normal moment identity E exp(aWt)=exp(a²t/2) makes the density expectation one. Substituting dW=dB−0.3dt leaves stock drift 0.02 and log drift 0.02−0.02=0. Award 1 for λ, 2 for normalization and 2 for the substituted dynamics.

    (d) Normalization establishes a probability law; positivity gives equivalence on this finite horizon. The construction must also establish the Brownian increment/filtration property and appropriate integrability for the relevant stochastic gains. A local martingale need not be a true martingale under arbitrary coefficients or strategies. Apply the square-integrable/admissible class actually justified rather than extending the result to every proposed model. Award 2 for the distinction, 2 for the additional conditions and 1 for scope.

  4. (a) The short options have delta −90 shares, so hold 90 shares. The mark approximation per option is 0.45(2)+½(0.02)(2²)+30(0.01)−5/250=1.22 CU. Short-option change is −244; fixed-stock change is +180; combined change is −64 CU. Award 1 for shares, 2 for the four terms and 2 for signs and combined value.

    (b) This abbreviated expression omits mixed/time/volatility curvature terms and higher remainders; its held-fixed coefficients need a valid local domain. Funded profit additionally needs initial cash, interest, dividends, executed resets, fees and settlement. A static mark calculation does not supply these cash flows. Award 2 for omitted mathematical terms, 2 for specific cash requirements and 1 for the conditional interpretation.

    (c) Raw SE is 6/√400=0.30; pair SE is 3/√200≈0.212132034. The corresponding estimated mean variances are 0.09 and 0.045, at the same 400 payoff evaluations. The 200 pairs, not their 400 dependent members, are the independent units. Award 2 for SEs, 1 for variances and 2 for units/equal-cost comparison. (d) Approximate half-widths are 0.588 and 0.415778787 CU. They concern sampling of each fixed estimator under its stated ideal assumptions, not contract error, discretization bias, changed model dynamics, selection or certainty of a profitable hedge. Award 2 for half-widths, 2 for distinct excluded errors and 1 for the fixed-sample/approximation qualification.

  5. (a) The forward is 50/0.95=1000/19. Let p₁=a. The stock restriction gives p₃−p₁=5/57, so p=(a,52/57−2a,a+5/57), with 0<a<26/57. The call costs 0.95·30(a+5/57)=5/2+(57/2)a, giving (2.5,15.5) CU. Award 2 for the calibrated vector, 1 for strict domain and 2 for the price interval.

    (b) The subhedge ST−50 pays (−30,0,30) and costs 50−0.95(50)=2.5. The superhedge 0.5ST−10 pays (0,15,30) and costs 15.5. At the lower endpoint buy the call and short its subhedge, receiving (30,0,0) at zero cost; at the upper buy the superhedge and short the call, receiving (0,15,0). Strict physical possibility makes both arbitrages. Award 2 for portfolios/costs, 2 for endpoint residuals and 1 for positivity.

    (c) The unit test passes, but book discrepancy is 12 CU and fails the eight-CU limit. At 400 units it is 8, passing the stated inclusive bound. Award 2 for unit/book distinction, 2 for quantities and 1 for boundary interpretation. (d) Reject the unreviewed-version request despite a valid size exception; a size permission cannot waive version binding or the outstanding book failure. The call's interval is a model-identification result, not a numerical error estimate. Selecting an interior price requires an additional valuation rule and scoped evidence. Bind the actual artifact and inputs, reconcile the price comparison or restrict exposure, and document the model-choice uncertainty and closure tests separately. Award 2 for the version decision, 2 for separating the three evidence claims and 1 for actionable scope/closure.

Notation index

SymbolMeaning and unitsPrimary route
D(t), z(t), fDiscount factor; annual continuously compounded zero rate; explicitly stated forward-rate conventionCash flows and curves
Duration, convexity, key-rate vectorFirst/second price response to a named rate coordinate; scaling convention must be statedRate hedges
P and QPhysical and selected pricing probability laws, respectivelyTerm-structure models, measure construction
τ, RrecDefault time and recovery fraction in credit; remaining maturity is separately labeled τ in vanilla pricingCredit, contractual cash
F, K, NForward delivery price, strike or specified delivery obligation, and notional or grid count as declared locallyForwards and swaps, options
W, Ft, [W]Brownian motion, information filtration and quadratic variationItô calculus
Δ, Γ, ν, ΘSpot delta, spot gamma, vega per unit volatility and calendar-time theta; multiply by signed contract unitsGreeks and funded hedging
h, k, SEDeclared spatial/time increments and sampling standard error; none is itself a model-error boundNumerical pricing
π, L, UPositive state-price vector and attainable sub/superhedge bounds in the declared marketIncomplete markets
E, G, εSigned comparison error, gross comparison amount and a tolerance with explicit units and interpretationModel governance

A symbol has only its stated local definition. In particular, q often denotes dividend yield in continuous pricing and a branch pricing probability in a finite tree; β can be a diffusion coefficient, a statistical coefficient or a numerical weight. Rewriting the local definitions is part of a correct derivation. Do not infer a common meaning from the same letter.

Concept index and targeted remediation

Observed failureRepair routeFresh evidence to produce
Wrong settlement, accrued interest or rate conventionChapter 1A dated cash ledger and independently reconstructed dirty/clean price or discount factors.
Duration treated as protection from every curve moveChapter 2, Chapter 3A parallel and a nonparallel scenario, with the exact coordinate, residual and physical/pricing interpretation.
Spread confused with physical default frequencyChapter 4A counterexample changing recovery, liquidity or a risk premium while preserving the observed spread.
Forward, futures, collateral and margin cash conflatedChapter 5A financed dated replication and a separate intermediate liquidity ledger.
Pricing probability guessed; exercise uses hindsightChapter 6Two-state matching equations or exhaustive small-tree adapted policies with the correct exercise rights.
Missing quadratic variation or unproved martingale stepChapter 7, Chapter 8A derivation naming filtration, regularity, measure and integrability before taking expectations.
Greek scale wrong; hedge reset silently injects cashChapter 9A signed multiplier check and every stock/dividend/bank/fee transfer, including terminal debt.
Fine grid or narrow confidence interval presented as full accuracyChapter 10Separate target, boundary, deterministic and sampling comparisons, with an applicable proof or an honest missing bound.
One exact model output treated as an identified priceChapter 11Alternative calibrated positive laws, a hedge interval or a contract-history counterexample.
Passing tests or a size exception treated as unrestricted permissionChapter 12A version-bound decision with material consequences, accountable owner, independent challenge and testable closure.

From conditional prices to an accountable valuation system

The volume begins with a dated cash claim. Curves assign present values; derivatives of those values expose local risks. Credit and funding change both the payments and the available trades. Finite replication gives a transparent pricing argument, while stochastic calculus explains which continuous gains a hedge can match. A pricing measure and PDE acquire financial meaning only through that cash, information and admissibility structure.

Greeks and numerical methods make the structure usable, with their own coordinates and errors. Discrete trading, uncertain volatility, additional drivers and contractual monitoring expose the limits of a single formula. In an incomplete market several positive pricing laws can agree on traded assets and disagree on another claim. Governance then asks which calculations have actually been verified, which values are identified or assumption-dependent, and what use the evidence can justify.

The diagnostic, written forms, project and oral transfers demand these connections rather than isolated formula recall. Their scoring thresholds, synthetic cases and review procedures are original instructional choices. They do not accredit the learner, guarantee exam or employment outcomes, or replace external review of professional judgment. Further research requires the broader convergence, semimartingale, calibration and empirical theories explicitly identified in the chapter extensions.

The planned Volume 11 places these tools inside banks and financial institutions: balance sheets, liquidity, counterparties, regulation and international exposures make the timing and model-use decisions consequential. Retain the completed pricing-and-risk evidence packet as an input to that study. Source catalogues and chapter links provide the scoped primary readings; successful code execution remains distinct from factual, mathematical, empirical and human performance review.
